faq.q: Why is H&E the first stain used?

faq.a: Malaria parasites are best seen in blood smears; tissue sections may show pigment but are not reliable for diagnosis.
faq.q: Can I diagnose malaria from tissue histology?

faq.a: Uniform pale cytoplasm often reflects viral infection or early fibrosis; context determines significance.

exam: A patient with chronic cough and weight loss has a lung biopsy showing caseating granulomas — what is the next diagnostic step? — Order sputum GeneXpert; if unavailable, start empirical anti‑TB therapy based on clinical score.

You see sheets of atypical lymphoid cells in a lymph node; how do you distinguish reactive hyperplasia from lymphoma? — Look for loss of nodal architecture, monoclonality on immunohistochemistry; if stains unavailable, correlate with systemic B‑symptoms.

A biopsy from a liver lesion shows eosinophilic granulomas with central necrosis; which tropical infection is most likely? — Schistosomiasis; treat with praziquantel and assess for portal hypertension.

In a patient with sickle‑cell disease, bone marrow shows hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia — what does this indicate? — Compensatory response to chronic haemolysis; monitor for aplastic crisis.

A skin punch biopsy shows spindle cells forming slit‑like vascular spaces; what condition should you consider and why is it relevant in HIV patients? — Kaposi sarcoma; it signals advanced immunosuppression and may need chemotherapy.

During a rapid autopsy, you cannot obtain special stains; how would you still identify TB in lung tissue? — Look for caseating necrosis, Langhans giant cells, and clinical history; start anti‑TB if suspicion high.

A patient on long‑term antiretroviral therapy presents with oral ulceration; biopsy shows viral cytopathic changes with Cowdry bodies — what virus is likely and what is the management implication? — HSV; start acyclovir and review immune status.

You notice loss of brush border in renal tubular cells on a biopsy; what functional defect does this explain and how does it guide treatment? — Impaired reabsorption leading to Fanconi‑type syndrome; manage with electrolyte replacement and avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
ai.title: Cell Histology
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Cell histology describes the microscopic structure of cells and their organelles, linking form to function. Understanding normal histology guides interpretation of tissue pathology in low‑resource settings.

b: Nucleus contains DNA, appears dark with H&E
Cytoplasm stains pink, shows organelles with special stains
Cell borders may be visible with PAS or trichrome
sections.p: Cells are the basic units of life. Histology uses light microscopy and simple stains (e.g., H&E) to visualise nuclei, cytoplasm, membranes and extracellular matrix.

b: Epithelial cells line surfaces; polarity (apical vs basal) matters for transport
Muscle cells contain many mitochondria and sarcoplasmic reticulum
Neurons have long axons and Nissl substance
sections.p: Different tissues have characteristic cell shapes: squamous (flat), cuboidal (cube‑shaped), columnar (tall) and transitional. Organelles vary with function – e.g., abundant rough ER in secretory cells.

b: Tight junctions prevent paracellular leak
Desmosomes provide mechanical strength
Gap junctions allow electrical coupling
sections.p: Cells interact with basement membrane, neighbouring cells via tight junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions, influencing barrier function and signal transmission.

b: Ischemia leads to loss of nuclear staining (coagulative necrosis)
Reperfusion may cause hemorrhagic transformation
sections.p: Capillary networks supply oxygen and nutrients; in low‑resource hospitals, tissue hypoxia is common in severe anaemia or sickle‑cell crises.

b: Denervation atrophy shows reduced cell size and cytoplasmic eosinophilia
sections.p: Sensory and autonomic fibres innervate many tissues; loss of innervation alters cell morphology (e.g., atrophic smooth muscle).

b: Goblet cells produce mucus seen as pale vacuoles
Podocytes have foot processes forming filtration slits
sections.p: Cell structure determines function: secretory granules in endocrine cells, cilia in respiratory epithelium, contractile filaments in muscle.

b: Granulomas with caseation suggest TB
Schistosome eggs cause eosinophilic granulomas in liver
HIV‑related Kaposi sarcoma shows spindle cells and vascular channels
sections.p: Histologic patterns help diagnose infections, malignancy and inflammatory diseases common in East Africa.

t.b: What basic tissue architecture looks like? – Shows cell size, nuclear features and overall pattern; if unavailable, use rapid Giemsa smear for cytology
Does acid‑fast bacilli exist? – Positive indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis; if not available, rely on clinical TB score and chest X‑ray
Is there fungal or glycogen‑rich material? – Highlights fungi (yeast buds) and basement membrane; if unavailable, use mucicarmine or consider clinical context

b: Look for nuclear pleomorphism and mitoses to suspect malignancy
Identify eosinophilic infiltrates for parasitic infection
Recognise loss of polarity in dysplasia
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, not memorising every cell type. Correlate microscopic findings with bedside clues (e.g., chronic cough → granulomas).

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive organ failure with histologic evidence of necrosis (e.g., fulminant hepatitis)
Severe sepsis with unidentified pathogen on tissue stain
Unexplained massive hemorrhage from tissue biopsy
